Yes. The lockfile has 65 entries, but only five packages are declared directly, and all five are used.

| Package | Where it's used |
|---|---|
| `react`, `react-dom` | `frontend/src` (5 `react` imports and 1 `react-dom/client` import) |
| `vite`, `@vitejs/plugin-react` | `frontend/vite.config.js` |
| `concurrently` | the root `npm run dev` script, which runs the API and web server together |

The other 60 or so are transitive dependencies that npm installs for those five. You can't remove them without removing the package that needs them.

- **Platform binaries (about 27):** `@rolldown/binding-*` (15) and `lightningcss-*` (11) come from Vite 8, plus `fsevents`. They are optional dependencies, one per OS and CPU. npm lists all of them in the lockfile so it is the same on every machine, but it only installs the one for your platform. Teammates on Mac, Windows and Linux all need their own entry.
- **`concurrently`'s tree (about 15):** `chalk`, `yargs`, `rxjs`, `tree-kill`, `shell-quote` and similar.
- **Vite's tree:** `rolldown`, `postcss`, `picomatch`, `fdir`, `tinyglobby`, `nanoid`, `lightningcss` and others.

The one thing you could drop is `concurrently`, which accounts for about 15 entries. You could do that by running the API and the frontend in two terminals. The `npm run dev` convenience probably isn't worth losing, so I'd keep it.

Keep `package-lock.json` committed. It pins exact versions so everyone gets the same install.

This is an environment problem, not a bug in the code. `slots=True` for dataclasses was added in Python 3.10, and [backend/README.md](backend/README.md) says the backend needs Python 3.10 or newer. Maggie's `python3` is probably 3.9, which is the Python that ships with macOS. Her traceback also shows that `.venv` isn't in the path, so she is likely using the system Python.

She can fix it like this:

```bash
python3 --version                # confirm it's 3.9 or lower
brew install python@3.12         # or any 3.10+ (python.org installer also works)

cd ~/sheridan-datathon/backend
rm -rf .venv
python3.12 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt
.venv/bin/python scripts/setup_db.py /path/to/data
```

`scripts/run-api.mjs` uses `backend/.venv` when it exists, so `npm run dev` will pick up the new venv.

I could instead drop `slots=True` from the four dataclasses in [backend/app/db/types.py](backend/app/db/types.py), which would run on 3.9. I'd advise against it. It only helps if nothing else in the backend needs 3.10, I haven't checked that, and the README already sets 3.10+ as the requirement. If you'd like the version requirement enforced, I can add a version check at the top of `setup_db.py`. It would fail with "Python 3.10+ required" instead of this traceback.

Both limits come from rules in the backend calculator, in [engine.py:117-125](backend/app/finance/engine.py#L117-L125). Each rule rejects some scenarios. When you stack scenarios, the combined one can break a rule even though each part passed on its own, so I had to choose how to handle it.

## Durations

Every scenario has a length, such as "lose my job for **3 months**" or "groceries go up for **6 months**". The calculator works out how much money you need for the whole scenario:

> money needed = one-off costs + (months × monthly shortfall)

It only takes **one** number of months. If income and costs have different lengths, it refuses with *"Different shock durations need separate scenarios"*. It can't model "no income for months 1–3, then income back but higher grocery costs until month 6".

**Example.** You apply "I lose my job for 3 months", then add "groceries rise $80/month for 6 months". The combined scenario has a 3 and a 6, which the calculator rejects. I picked the **longest**, so the combined scenario becomes "no income **and** +$80 groceries for 6 months".

This is cautious: it overstates the job loss by 3 months, so it asks you to save more than you strictly need. Using the shortest would understate the grocery costs and make you look safer than you are. The review card adds a note when this happens, so you see the change before you apply it.

The real fix is to teach the calculator about overlapping time periods, which is a backend change. I can do that if this approximation matters for your demo.

## Overlap check

The calculator also guards against counting the same money twice. Two cases trigger it:
- a **household bills %** change together with a specific cost whose name mentions rent, mortgage, utilities, bills or household;
- an **overall spending %** change together with any specific category cost.

**Example.** "Bills rise 10%" and "rent goes up $200/month" might describe the same rent increase. Applying both could double-count it. So the calculator refuses unless the scenario carries a flag saying the user confirmed they're separate (`overlap_acknowledged`). For a single message, the app asks you that question with a checkbox before you can apply.

When stacking, you could apply "bills rise 10%" and later add "rent goes up $200". Neither message overlaps on its own, so you were never asked. Combined, they trip the check and the apply would just fail with an error you can't answer.

I chose to set the flag automatically on combined scenarios. My reasoning was that you deliberately added each part, so you meant them to stack. The downside is that if you did mean the same rent increase twice, the app won't catch it and the shortfall will be overstated.

The safer alternative is to ask the checkbox question again whenever stacking creates a new overlap. I can switch to that if you'd prefer.

def stacked_schedule(shock: Shock, income: float, spending: float, bills: float) -> list[tuple[float, float]]:
    """Month-by-month (income, spending) for stacked parts, each applied only during its own window.

    Every part starts in month 1; permanent parts (no duration) last the whole horizon. Income
    multipliers multiply; spending changes add, each measured against the baseline.

    deltas = []
    for p in shock.parts:
        if p.parts:
            raise ValueError("Stacked scenarios cannot be nested.")
        inc, sp = _apply_single(p, income, spending, bills)   # also validates the part on its own
        factor = p.income_multiplier if p.income_multiplier is not None else 1.0
        deltas.append((p.window, factor, sp - spending))
    horizon = max((w for w, _, _ in deltas if w), default=1)
    schedule = []
    for month in range(1, horizon + 1):

        schedule.append((month_income, month_spending))

"""Stacked scenarios: each part applies only for its own duration, assessed month by month."""
import pytest

from app.finance.engine import RecurringCost, Shock, build_plan
from app.finance.planning import PlanningOptions
from app.main import ShockModel

BASE = {"income": 3000, "spending": 2600, "buffer": 5200, "household_bills": 900, "months_of_history": 40}
FLEX = {"card_withdrawals": 420}

# No income for 2 months, plus +$400/month of costs for 4 months.
JOB_LOSS = Shock(income_multiplier=0, income_duration_months=2)
COSTS = Shock(recurring_costs=[RecurringCost("Childcare", 400)], scenario_duration_months=4)


def test_each_part_applies_only_for_its_own_window():
    p = build_plan(BASE, FLEX, Shock(parts=[JOB_LOSS, COSTS]), planning=PlanningOptions())
    d = p["duration_assessment"]
    # Months 1-2: 0 in, 3000 out. Months 3-4: 3000 in, 3000 out. Deepest point: -6000.
    assert d["months"] == 4
    assert d["buffer_path"] == [5200, 2200, -800, -800, -800]
    assert d["required_starting_buffer"] == 6000      # not 4 x 3000 = 12000 if both lasted 4 months
    assert d["additional_buffer_needed"] == 800
    assert d["ending_buffer"] == -800
    assert d["covers_duration"] is False
    # Month 1 is the snapshot: every part in effect.
    assert p["after_shock"]["income"] == 0 and p["after_shock"]["spending"] == 3000
    # A flat cut of 400/month keeps the buffer at zero or above through month 2, the worst point.
    assert p["backup_plan"]["monthly_cut_needed"] == 400
    backup = p["action_plan"]["backup"]
    assert backup["additional_monthly_improvement_needed"] == 400
    assert backup["additional_buffer_for_horizon"] == 800
    assert backup["ending_buffer_after_actions"] == -800
    assert backup["covers_duration_after_actions"] is False
    assert p["shock"]["label"] == "Income at 0% of normal for 2 months; Childcare +400/month (user_estimate) for 4 months"


def test_confirmed_cut_covers_stacked_horizon():
    p = build_plan(BASE, FLEX, Shock(parts=[JOB_LOSS, COSTS]), planning=PlanningOptions(confirmed_monthly_cut=400))
    backup = p["action_plan"]["backup"]
    assert backup["covers_duration_after_actions"] is True
    assert backup["status"] == "covered"
    assert backup["ending_buffer_after_actions"] == 800      # 5200 - 2 x 2600 + 2 x 400


def test_parts_sharing_one_window_match_the_single_shock():
    single = Shock(income_multiplier=0.55, income_duration_months=6, household_bills_pct_change=10,
                   scenario_duration_months=6)
    stacked = Shock(parts=[Shock(income_multiplier=0.55, income_duration_months=6),
                           Shock(household_bills_pct_change=10, scenario_duration_months=6)])
    a = build_plan(BASE, FLEX, single, planning=PlanningOptions())
    b = build_plan(BASE, FLEX, stacked, planning=PlanningOptions())
    for key in ("after_shock", "duration_assessment", "backup_plan", "goal_plan", "action_plan"):
        assert a[key] == b[key]


def test_permanent_part_lasts_the_whole_horizon():
    p = build_plan(BASE, FLEX, Shock(parts=[JOB_LOSS, Shock(household_bills_pct_change=100)]))
    # Months 1-2: 0 in, 3500 out; months 3+: 3000 in, 3500 out, over a 2-month horizon.
    assert p["duration_assessment"]["months"] == 2
    assert p["duration_assessment"]["required_starting_buffer"] == 7000


def test_each_part_is_still_validated_on_its_own():
    bad = Shock(household_bills_pct_change=10, recurring_costs=[RecurringCost("Rent", 200)])
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="overlap"):
        build_plan(BASE, FLEX, Shock(parts=[JOB_LOSS, bad]))


def test_api_model_accepts_parts_but_not_nesting():
    m = ShockModel(parts=[{"income_multiplier": 0, "income_duration_months": 2},
                          {"recurring_costs": [{"label": "Childcare", "monthly_change": 400}],
                           "scenario_duration_months": 4}])
    shock = m.to_engine()
    assert len(shock.parts) == 2 and shock.parts[1].window == 4
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        ShockModel(parts=[{"parts": [{"income_multiplier": 0}]}])

The calculator now gives each stacked scenario its own duration, the chart sits at about 60% width with the four cards stacked beside it, and text sizes now follow one scale. The backend tests pass (165, including 6 new ones for stacked scenarios) and the frontend builds. I haven't looked at any of this in a browser, so check the layout and sizes yourself.

**Durations:** You were right that the idea is simple. The calculator now works out each month separately, with each scenario active only for its own number of months. For example, "no income for 2 months" plus "+$400/month for 4 months" gives:
- months 1–2: no income, $400 extra costs;
- months 3–4: income back, $400 extra costs.

You now need $6,000 instead of the $12,000 the old "use the longest duration" approach gave. The figures that depended on one constant gap now work month by month too:
- the required buffer, the ending balance and the suggested monthly cut;
- the backup plan's figures.

A scenario with no duration counts for the whole period. When every part has the same duration, the calculator uses the original formulas, so single-scenario results are exactly as before.

In the frontend, each applied scenario is now sent as its own part instead of being merged into one. The review card lists each change with its own duration, and the chart follows the real month-by-month balance. The before/after table shows month 1, when every change is active, and the outcome box now says so. You can stack up to 10 changes; after that the chat asks you to reload the account.

The overlap check now runs within each scenario but not between scenarios, which is the same behaviour I described before.

**Chart:** It takes about 60% of the width and is about 10% taller than it was at full width. The four cards are stacked on its right at matching height. On narrow screens they drop below the chart.

**Text sizes:** All the smaller sizes are replaced by one scale, defined at the end of [styles.css](frontend/src/styles.css):

| Role | Size | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Section headings | 28px | "Describe a change", "See the impact" |
| Subtitles | 22px | "Plain language in. Clear assumptions out." |
| Card headings | 20px | "Buffer through the scenario" |
| Body text | 16px | chat, tables, explanations |
| Supporting text | 14px | notes, help text, form labels |
| Captions | 12px | eyebrows, table headers, footer |
| Big numbers | 26px | metric and card values |

I treated the grey lines under headings as the subtitles. Most were 11px, so 22px is the 100% increase. I raised section headings to 28px so they stay larger than their subtitles. If you meant the headings themselves, tell me and I'll swap them.

The base text size went from 14px to 16px across the whole app, and on phones the larger sizes step down a bit. I removed the Stress-Test-only size overrides, since the shared scale now covers them.
